prompt: A surprise expense appeared after you made your plan. Which idea best explains why some plans handled it better?

options.text: Plans with some savings kept as a buffer could pay without borrowing.
The plans that spent everything were just unlucky.
Borrowing is always the cheapest way to handle a surprise.

prompt: Why does a good budget cover needs before wants?

options.text: Needs like transport and food cannot be skipped without real consequences.
Wants are always bad and should never be bought.
The order does not matter if the total is the same.

prompt: You wanted to save for a goal. What most increased your chance of reaching it?

options.text: Setting aside a fixed amount early in the month, before spending on wants.
Hoping there would be money left at the end of the month.
Spending freely and saving only if the goal is cheap.

prompt: Why keep an emergency fund separate from your goal savings?

options.text: So an emergency does not force you to raid, or give up on, your goal.
Because emergencies never happen if you plan well.
Because one big pot always earns more interest.

prompt: Why does compound interest grow faster than simple interest over time?

options.text: Interest is earned on earlier interest as well as on the original amount.
Because the bank pays a higher rate for compound interest.
Because you must add more money each month.

prompt: Which habit made the biggest difference to your savings result?

options.text: Saving a regular amount every month and not touching it.
Saving a very large amount once, then stopping.
Keeping the money in cash at home so it is easy to spend.

prompt: Why does spreading money across different baskets reduce risk?

options.text: When one thing falls, others may hold up, so one bad outcome cannot sink everything.
Because every basket always grows at the same rate.
Because single companies are guaranteed to do better.

prompt: If you need money in one year, what is the sensible way to think about risk?

options.text: Choose steadier options, because a fall may not have time to recover.
Choose the riskiest option to grow quickly.
Time makes no difference to risk.

prompt: The market fell during your simulation. What is the most useful lesson?

options.text: Falls are normal; what matters is whether you needed the money soon and how calmly you react.
A fall proves investing is a scam.
You should always sell at the first sign of a fall.

prompt: Why should you never share an OTP or PIN, even with someone claiming to be from your bank?

options.text: Genuine banks never ask for them; anyone who does is trying to move your money.
Because sharing is only risky if the caller sounds rude.
Because OTPs are only needed to receive money.

prompt: What is the strongest warning sign in a message that says 'Act in 10 minutes or lose your money'?

options.text: Urgency. Scammers rush you so you will not stop to check.
The message uses capital letters.
It came on a weekend.

prompt: A message promises to triple your money in a month. What should you conclude?

options.text: Guaranteed high returns do not exist; this is a classic scam pattern.
It is probably fine if a friend forwarded it.
Try it with a small amount first to see.

prompt: By month six the earphones cost more than they did at the start. What does that show?

options.text: Prices rise over time, so money that earns nothing buys a little less later.
The shop made a mistake.
Saving is pointless because prices always win.

prompt: Why did money that was 'kept ready' make the surprise easier?

options.text: It was available instantly with no loss, which is what liquidity means.
Cash always earns the most interest.
Surprises only matter if you have no goal.

prompt: Why is putting most of the ₹500 in the growth basket risky for a goal six months away?

options.text: A poor period can shrink it, and there may not be time to recover before you need the money.
Because the growth basket always loses money.
Because deposits never lose value to inflation.
